title: Hudson Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hudson wells have a 70-foot median depth, but 33% are deeper than 600 feet. See yields, water levels, costs and local risks.
h1: Hudson, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Hudson means looking past the presence of a well. The local record includes 1,814 permitted wells within 5 miles, but only 926 are recorded as constructed, 1,109 report a total depth, and 430 report a pump yield. That makes the available data useful for local planning, but not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Hudson sits on the plains over the Denver Basin. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells throughout this area, with many records tied to unnamed or fractured-bedrock, Laramie Fox Hills, and alluvial aquifers. Neighboring-well records, the permit file, water rights, and a site-specific driller's estimate all matter before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Hudson well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
The reported median well depth near Hudson is 70 feet. The middle half of recorded wells runs from 40 to 740 feet, which is an unusually wide planning range. A shallow median does not mean every lot will have a shallow bid: 33% of wells are 600 feet or deeper, while 55% are under 100 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,700 feet.

For a buyer, ask the driller to explain which nearby wells are genuinely comparable. Depth can change with the targeted Denver Basin formation, local sedimentary bedrock conditions, water-quality needs, and the intended use. Do not use the median alone to set a drilling allowance. A bid based on nearby deep wells may be more useful than one based on the local average.

sections.heading: Most Hudson wells report useful production, but confirm the test
sections.html:
Among the 430 records reporting a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half falls between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is stronger than many buyers expect: 63% report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 36% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, and 2% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

These are permit-record figures, not a promise for a new well. Ask for the actual well test, sustained rate, recovery information, storage capacity, and pump design. Household demand, livestock, irrigation, and fire-protection needs are different. A good reported yield still needs to be matched to the legal permit and the proposed use.

sections.heading: Hudson water levels show a deeper recent pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 220 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 20 to 430 feet. Measurements by decade were 140 feet in the 1970s, 18 feet in the 1990s, 20 feet in the 2000s, 378 feet in the 2010s, and 344 feet in the 2020s.

That series suggests recorded water levels were substantially deeper in the later measurement decades than in the earlier records. It does not prove a uniform decline across every part of Hudson. The wells measured, aquifers, seasons, and measurement methods may differ. For a purchase, compare the subject well with nearby wells in the same aquifer and ask for a current static level. Pump setting, pressure-tank sizing, and trench planning should account for the actual site conditions.

sections.heading: Hudson's permit history identifies the active drillers
sections.html:
Permitting has continued near Hudson through 2025. The largest permit decade was the 2000s, with 524 permits. The record shows 236 in the 2010s and 166 in the 2020s, compared with 217 in the 1990s. Older records include 88 permits in the 1950s, 79 in the 1960s, 99 in the 1970s, and 95 in the 1980s.

The most active drillers named in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 243 wells, Holden & Holden (Holden, B L) with 127, and Crandall Drilling & Pump Service (Crandall Jr., Howard H.) with 81. Treat that list as permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, scope, and references before signing.

sections.heading: A Hudson well can cost more than the hole itself
sections.html:
For Hudson's Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the planning rate is about $50 to $70 per foot. At the local median depth of 70 feet, the drilled hole works out to roughly $3,500 to $4,900. That is only the drilling portion in the model. A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at about $9,500 to $16,900.

The wide depth distribution is the main reason not to rely on the median when budgeting. A new-well proposal should state the included depth, casing and grout, pump, pressure equipment, electrical work, trench length, testing, and any difficult-ground charges. Ask what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected. Also verify the permit and intended use before authorizing construction; an exempt household-use well still has legal limits, including the 35 gallons-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: Hudson buyers need to check water, septic, and the building site
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention. Mapping shows 893 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Hudson, along with 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped sites do not establish contamination in a particular well. They do justify reviewing available sampling, testing the existing well, and checking the location and history of the property before closing. Test results should be interpreted for the intended household use.

Low yield, a dry hole, a deep static level, and poor recovery are separate risks. So are septic setbacks, drainfield soil, access for a rig, electrical service, and room for a future replacement system. A permitted well may serve domestic, stock, irrigation, or monitoring purposes; the local mix is 50% domestic or household, 16% stock, 14% irrigation, and 19% monitoring. Confirm that the permit matches your plan and check augmentation requirements in any over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Hudson
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit file, then compare the subject property with nearby records in Hudson and the surrounding areas of Keenesburg, Aristocrat Ranchettes, and Lochbuie. Look for wells targeting the same aquifer, similar depths, comparable uses, and actual yield and water-level data. A map alone cannot tell you whether a parcel will produce a reliable household supply.

For an existing home, obtain the well permit, construction report, pump details, recent water test, and a current flow or recovery assessment. For vacant land, make the driller walk the access route and proposed well location before pricing the work. Coordinate well, septic, driveway, and building locations together. If the planned use exceeds an exempt household-use permit, obtain water-rights advice early; an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hudson, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Hudson is 70 feet. The middle half ranges from 40 to 740 feet, so local conditions vary widely. Fifty-five percent are under 100 feet, while 33% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 1,700 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hudson, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 70-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,500 to $4,900. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,500 to $16,900. A site-specific bid can differ substantially because depths range widely.

faq.q: How much water do Hudson wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 430 local records reporting a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-three percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 36% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Confirm the actual test for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hudson, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that any particular well is safe to drink. About 10 miles around Hudson contains 893 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test an existing or new well for relevant contaminants, review the property history, and use qualified guidance to interpret results.

faq.q: Are Hudson well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Recorded median static water levels were 140 feet below ground in the 1970s, 18 feet in the 1990s, 20 feet in the 2000s, 378 feet in the 2010s, and 344 feet in the 2020s. This suggests deeper later measurements, but it does not prove a uniform decline because wells and measurement conditions differ.
